subChunks.title: The Utility Mindset
subChunks.hookHtml: Every senior front-end developer has a moment when they stop writing custom CSS for each new element and realise that utility-first CSS is faster, more consistent, and far easier to maintain. That moment starts here.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Why utility-first wins

Traditional CSS workflows ask you to do two jobs at once: design the element and invent a name for it. The name ends up in two files — the HTML and the stylesheet — and they must stay in sync forever. Rename one, the other breaks silently.

/* styles.css — the old way */
.profile-card-header-meta-subtitle {
  font-size: 0.875rem;
  color: #6b7280;
  margin-top: 4px;
}

Utility-first removes the naming step entirely. You compose small, single-purpose classes directly on the element:

<p class="text-sm text-gray-500 mt-1">Senior Engineer</p>

Same result. No extra file. No name to maintain.

How does this compare to other approaches?

  • Plain CSS / CSS Modules — maximum flexibility, but you write every value yourself, there's no shared constraint, and design inconsistencies creep in over time.
  • CSS-in-JS (styled-components, Emotion) — co-location is nice, but runtime cost, bundle bloat, and SSR complexity add up fast in production.
  • Semantic CSS (BEM) — disciplined naming helps, but you still maintain two files and the abstraction breaks when the design changes.
  • Tailwind — every token (colour, spacing, type size) is shared across the whole project. Changing the design system means changing one config file, not hundreds of classes.

The property-value naming pattern

Every Tailwind class follows the same pattern: property-value. Once you know the pattern, you can guess new classes before you look them up.

bg-blue-500      /* background-color: rgb(59 130 246)   */
text-white       /* color: rgb(255 255 255)              */
p-4              /* padding: 1rem (16px)                 */
px-6             /* padding-left + right: 1.5rem (24px)  */
rounded-lg       /* border-radius: 0.5rem               */
font-semibold    /* font-weight: 600                    */
shadow-md        /* box-shadow: medium preset           */

Using Tailwind in React

React uses className, not class. This is the only HTML difference you need to remember.

// HTML
<div class="bg-white p-6 rounded-xl shadow-md">

// JSX (React)
<div className="bg-white p-6 rounded-xl shadow-md">

In real React projects you'll also use the clsx or cn utility to conditionally combine classes:

import clsx from 'clsx';

function Button({ primary, children }) {
  return (
    <button
      className={clsx(
        'px-4 py-2 rounded-md font-medium',
        primary ? 'bg-blue-600 text-white' : 'bg-gray-100 text-gray-900'
      )}
    >
      {children}
    </button>
  );
}

Building a stat card

A stat card is a classic UI component: a container with a label and a big number. Here is what we are building:

<div class="stat-card">
  <p class="stat-label">Total Students</p>
  <p class="stat-value">12,847</p>
</div>

The card needs: a white or light background, padding on all sides, rounded corners, and a subtle shadow. The label needs small muted text. The value needs large bold text. Apply those utilities now.

storyBeats.text: You step into the Academy's Scriptorium — a vast hall lined with glowing runes. Enchanters inscribe visual spells onto parchment, each working at a lectern. Scrolls are everywhere: some filled with long incantations, others covered in tiny, precise symbols. Lyra the Scribe glances up from a stack of them.

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: Ah — a new apprentice. Let me guess: you have been writing bespoke names for every scroll you produce? .card-header-title-special, .button-blue-thing-v2? And now you have two scrolls per element — one for the name, one for the spell — and they must stay in sync forever?

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: The Academy abandoned that tradition years ago. We use glyphs instead: small, single-purpose symbols, each doing exactly one thing. You compose them directly on the element. No inventing names. No second scroll. No synchronisation.

storyBeats.speaker: Old way vs. utility-first — side by side

storyBeats.text: You study the two blocks side by side. The old way names a concept — profile-card — and then defines it elsewhere. The new way is the definition. There is nothing to name, nothing to look up. The HTML and the style are the same sentence.

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: You see it. Good. The moment you stop inventing names, you stop maintaining two files. Rename the element? There is nothing to rename — the glyphs are the element. Delete the element? The styles vanish with it. No orphaned CSS, no dead code.

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: Every glyph follows the same pattern: property-value. Learn the pattern once and you can read — or write — any glyph you encounter. bg-blue-500: background, blue, shade 500. text-sm: text size, small. rounded-lg: border-radius, large. No guessing. No documentation hunting. Now — apply that instinct to the stat card below.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Style this stat card component. Apply the following utilities:

  • .stat-card: bg-white, p-6, rounded-xl, shadow-md, border, border-gray-100
  • .stat-label: text-sm, text-gray-500, font-medium
  • .stat-value: text-3xl, font-bold, text-gray-900, mt-1
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Style this stat card from scratch — no hints about which classes to use. Apply what you know about Tailwind utilities to produce a clean, professional card:

  • The .stat-card container needs a white background, comfortable padding on all sides, large rounded corners, a subtle shadow, and a thin border.
  • The .stat-label should be small text in a muted colour, medium-weight.
  • The .stat-value should be a very large, bold number in near-black, with a small top margin to separate it from the label.

Don't look at the guided practice unless you truly need to.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain utility-first CSS to a developer who has only ever used BEM and CSS Modules. Cover: why you do not need to invent class names, how the design system stays consistent, and one scenario where you would still write custom CSS despite using Tailwind.

questions.questionHtml: Which Tailwind class sets a medium box shadow?
questions.explanationHtml: Shadow utilities follow shadow-{size}: shadow-sm, shadow (default), shadow-md, shadow-lg, shadow-xl, shadow-2xl, shadow-inner, shadow-none.

questions.questionHtml: In JSX (React), how do you apply Tailwind classes to an element?
questions.explanationHtml: React requires className instead of class because class is a reserved word in JavaScript. Every other aspect of Tailwind usage is identical to plain HTML.

questions.questionHtml: You want a card with: white background, 24 px of padding, large rounded corners, and a subtle shadow. Which class string is correct?
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind classes are plain strings separated by spaces in the class or className attribute. No leading dots (those are CSS selectors, not class values), no raw CSS property names.

questions.questionHtml: A developer writes className={`bg-${color}-500`} where color is a string from an API response. What problem will they encounter?
options: The class will never apply because Tailwind cannot detect dynamically interpolated class names at build time
It works fine — Tailwind handles template literals automatically
It works in development but is slightly slower in production
The class applies but the colour shade will default to 500
questions.correctAnswer: The class will never apply because Tailwind cannot detect dynamically interpolated class names at build time
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind scans source files for complete class name strings. bg-blue-500 is found; bg-${color}-500 is not — no part of it is a valid complete class. The fix is a lookup map: const colourMap = { blue: 'bg-blue-500', red: 'bg-red-500' }, then use colourMap[color]. This is one of the most common Tailwind gotchas in real projects.

questions.questionHtml:
Your team is debating CSS strategies for a new React project. One engineer argues for CSS Modules (one .module.css file per component). Another prefers Tailwind. The design uses a consistent 8-point spacing scale and a fixed palette of 12 brand colours.

Which argument most accurately represents an advantage of Tailwind in this specific context?
options: Tailwind enforces the spacing scale and colour palette automatically through its token system, making design drift structurally impossible without config changes
Tailwind is faster to type than CSS Modules
CSS Modules cannot implement the same design system
Tailwind generates smaller CSS files in all cases
questions.correctAnswer: Tailwind enforces the spacing scale and colour palette automatically through its token system, making design drift structurally impossible without config changes
questions.explanationHtml: When a design uses a fixed palette and spacing scale, Tailwind's config is a direct representation of that system. Every developer on the team can only use values that exist in the config — there is nowhere to sneak in an arbitrary color: #e74c3c or margin: 13px. CSS Modules give each developer a blank canvas, which means design drift requires discipline rather than tooling. Neither approach produces smaller CSS in all cases (JIT is very efficient, but a module that is never loaded costs nothing too). This is the key architectural advantage Tailwind provides.

subChunks.title: Setup for Vite + React
subChunks.hookHtml: Ninety percent of new React projects today use Vite. Tailwind v4 made setup dramatically simpler: two commands, one CSS import, no config file. Understanding the setup sequence — and the one scanning rule that can still catch you out — is a genuine job-readiness skill.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Installing Tailwind v4 in a Vite + React project

Two commands. No config file. No PostCSS setup required.

# 1. Create the project (if you haven't already)
npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts
cd my-app

# 2. Install Tailwind and its Vite plugin
npm install -D tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite

Configure the Vite plugin

Open vite.config.ts and register the Tailwind plugin:

import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'
import tailwindcss from '@tailwindcss/vite'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    react(),
    tailwindcss(),  // ← this is the entire Tailwind setup
  ],
})

No postcss.config.js required. The Vite plugin handles compilation, scanning, and hot-reload internally.

Import Tailwind in your CSS

Replace all contents of src/index.css with a single line:

@import "tailwindcss";

That single import replaces the three @tailwind base/components/utilities directives from v3. Import the file in src/main.tsx:

import './index.css';

Automatic content detection

Tailwind v4 scans your project files automatically — no content array to configure or maintain. For the vast majority of Vite + React projects you are fully set up at this point.

The one edge case: if you use a component library in node_modules that ships Tailwind classes in its source, add an explicit @source directive:

@import "tailwindcss";

/* Scan a third-party UI library */
@source "../node_modules/@my-org/ui/src/**/*.tsx";

The dynamic class trap — still applies in v4

Automatic detection changed how file paths are found. It did not change how class names are found. Tailwind v4 is still a text scanner — every class string must appear verbatim in a scanned file.

// BROKEN — 'bg-blue-500' never appears as a complete string in source
const cls = `bg-${colour}-500`;

// CORRECT — full strings are visible in source
const colourMap = {
  blue:  'bg-blue-500',
  red:   'bg-red-500',
  green: 'bg-green-500',
};
const cls = colourMap[colour];

This is still the most common Tailwind bug in production code. When you see it in a code review, flag it immediately.

Safelisting classes from external data

When class names come from a CMS, database, or API and cannot appear verbatim in source, use @source inline() in your CSS:

/* Safelist explicit class names */
@source inline("bg-red-500 bg-green-500 text-red-800 text-green-800");

/* Pattern syntax for a whole family */
@source inline("{bg,text}-{red,green,blue}-{100,500,900}");

Using Tailwind in React (className, not class)

React uses className, not class. This is the only HTML syntax difference you need to remember:

// HTML
<div class="bg-white p-6 rounded-xl shadow-md">

// JSX (React)
<div className="bg-white p-6 rounded-xl shadow-md">

Verifying the setup

Run npm run dev and add className="bg-blue-500 text-white p-4" to any element. Blue box with white text = setup is correct.

storyBeats.text: Lyra leads you through a heavy door into a workshop. A broad-shouldered mage in a leather apron looks up from a workbench covered in tools.

storyBeats.speaker: Maester Cordell
storyBeats.text: Ah — new apprentice. Cordell. The Foundry. In the old days, setting up Tailwind meant three tools, a config file, and a content array. Tailwind v4 changed all of that. Two commands and one CSS import — that is the entire setup.

storyBeats.speaker: The two installation commands
storyBeats.text: npm install -D tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite

storyBeats.speaker: Maester Cordell
storyBeats.text: Add the Tailwind plugin to vite.config.ts. Then put a single line in your CSS file: @import "tailwindcss". No config file. No PostCSS configuration. No content array. Tailwind detects your source files automatically.

storyBeats.speaker: The entire CSS setup — one line
storyBeats.text: @import "tailwindcss";

storyBeats.speaker: Maester Cordell
storyBeats.text: Now — the one trap that did not change. The scanner reads your source files as plain text. If a complete class string does not appear verbatim in a scanned file, that class does not exist in production. Automatic detection removed the path configuration. It did not remove the scanning rule.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
The setup is already correct in this sandbox. Practice applying classes to a "setup confirmation" panel — the point is to reinforce that class application is all that remains once the toolchain is configured.

Style the elements:

  • .setup-panel: bg-slate-50, border, border-slate-200, rounded-lg, p-6
  • .setup-title: text-lg, font-semibold, text-slate-900
  • .setup-status: text-sm, text-green-600, font-medium, mt-2
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
Tailwind Configured

All systems operational
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Style this configuration panel from scratch — remember the class names without looking them up.

  • The .setup-panel needs a light slate background, a visible border, matching border colour, rounded corners, and comfortable all-around padding.
  • The .setup-title should be large text, semi-bold, in a dark slate colour.
  • The .setup-status should be small, green, medium-weight text with a top margin to separate it from the title.

Use the bg-slate-*, border-slate-*, text-slate-*, and text-green-* palettes you learned.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk through the complete setup sequence for Tailwind v4 in a brand-new Vite + React TypeScript project, from the first npm command to the point where you can verify styles are working. Explain what @tailwindcss/vite does, what @import 'tailwindcss' replaces, and what the one production trap is that still exists despite automatic content detection.

questions.questionHtml: What is the single CSS declaration needed to activate all of Tailwind v4 in your stylesheet?
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind v4 replaces the three @tailwind directives from v3 with a single standard CSS @import. This one line activates the base reset, all utility classes, and the theme system.

questions.questionHtml: Which npm package provides the Vite plugin for Tailwind v4?
questions.explanationHtml: @tailwindcss/vite is a dedicated first-party Vite plugin. It replaces the PostCSS pipeline from v3, handling compilation, scanning, and HMR in one plugin. You no longer need postcss.config.js, autoprefixer, or a separate tailwindcss PostCSS entry.

questions.questionHtml: How does Tailwind v4 determine which source files to scan for utility class names?
options: Automatically — v4 detects project files without any configuration
Via the content array in tailwind.config.js
By reading the import graph from your main.tsx entry file
questions.correctAnswer: Automatically — v4 detects project files without any configuration
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind v4 removed the need for a content array entirely. It automatically detects and scans your project files. For edge cases — such as a component library in node_modules — you can add an explicit @source directive to your CSS file.

questions.questionHtml: A developer writes const cls = `bg-${colour}-500` where colour comes from a prop. The class never applies in production despite Tailwind v4's automatic detection. Why?
options: Tailwind still scans as plain text — complete class strings must appear verbatim; 'bg-blue-500' is never a complete string in source
Automatic detection does not scan component props or variables
Template literals require a @source inline() entry to be detected
v4's Vite plugin only scans .tsx files, not dynamic expressions
questions.correctAnswer: Tailwind still scans as plain text — complete class strings must appear verbatim; 'bg-blue-500' is never a complete string in source
questions.explanationHtml: Automatic detection changed which files are scanned, not how class names are found. The scanner still performs text matching — bg-blue-500 must appear as a complete string somewhere in a scanned file. A template literal like `bg-${colour}-500` produces only the fragments bg- and -500. The fix is a lookup object: const map = { blue: 'bg-blue-500', red: 'bg-red-500' }.

questions.questionHtml: A team is upgrading an existing Vite + React app from Tailwind v3 to v4. They currently have a tailwind.config.js, a postcss.config.js, and the three @tailwind directives in their CSS. What is the correct migration sequence?
options: Install @tailwindcss/vite, add it to vite.config.ts, replace the three @tailwind directives with @import 'tailwindcss', move theme customisations to @theme {} in CSS, delete tailwind.config.js and postcss.config.js
Just upgrade the tailwindcss package to v4 — it is backward compatible with v3 configuration files
Delete tailwind.config.js and postcss.config.js without adding any replacement — v4 needs nothing
Replace the content array globs with @source directives but keep everything else identical
questions.correctAnswer: Install @tailwindcss/vite, add it to vite.config.ts, replace the three @tailwind directives with @import 'tailwindcss', move theme customisations to @theme {} in CSS, delete tailwind.config.js and postcss.config.js
questions.explanationHtml: The v4 migration has four parts: (1) swap the PostCSS pipeline for @tailwindcss/vite, (2) replace the three @tailwind directives with @import "tailwindcss", (3) migrate any theme customisations from tailwind.config.js into @theme {} blocks in your CSS, and (4) delete the now-redundant config and PostCSS files. The utility class API is largely unchanged — most component classes keep working without modification.

subChunks.title: The Spacing System
subChunks.hookHtml: Tailwind's spacing scale is the single most-used part of the framework. Master it and you can build any layout without writing a single pixel value — every gap, margin, and padding comes from the same shared system.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The 4px base unit

Every spacing value in Tailwind is a multiple of 4px (0.25rem). The number in the class name is the multiplier:

p-0   →  0px
p-1   →  4px   (0.25rem)
p-2   →  8px   (0.5rem)
p-3   →  12px  (0.75rem)
p-4   →  16px  (1rem)     ← the most common default
p-5   →  20px  (1.25rem)
p-6   →  24px  (1.5rem)
p-8   →  32px  (2rem)
p-10  →  40px  (2.5rem)
p-12  →  48px  (3rem)
p-16  →  64px  (4rem)
p-20  →  80px  (5rem)
p-24  →  96px  (6rem)

Padding variants

p-4      /* all four sides */
px-4     /* left + right (horizontal) */
py-4     /* top + bottom (vertical)   */
pt-4     /* top only    */
pr-4     /* right only  */
pb-4     /* bottom only */
pl-4     /* left only   */

Margin variants

m-4      /* all four sides */
mx-4     /* left + right   */
my-4     /* top + bottom   */
mt-4     /* top only       */
mr-4     /* right only     */
mb-4     /* bottom only    */
ml-4     /* left only      */
mx-auto  /* auto left+right — centres a block element horizontally */

Centering with mx-auto

mx-auto is the Tailwind equivalent of margin: 0 auto. Pair it with a max-w-* class to create a centred content column:

<div class="max-w-3xl mx-auto px-6">
  <!-- page content -->
</div>

Width constraints: max-w-*

max-w-xs    →  320px
max-w-sm    →  384px
max-w-md    →  448px
max-w-lg    →  512px
max-w-xl    →  576px
max-w-2xl   →  672px
max-w-3xl   →  768px
max-w-4xl   →  896px
max-w-5xl   →  1024px
max-w-6xl   →  1152px
max-w-7xl   →  1280px  ← common page width
max-w-prose →  65ch    ← optimal reading width
max-w-full  →  100%
max-w-screen → 100vw

Gap for flex and grid children

gap-* sets the gutter between flex or grid children. Prefer gap-* over margins on individual children — it is symmetric and easier to change:

<div class="flex gap-4">
  <div>Item 1</div>
  <div>Item 2</div>
  <div>Item 3</div>
</div>

gap-x-4   /* horizontal gap only */
gap-y-4   /* vertical gap only   */

Space between siblings: space-x-* and space-y-*

Adds margin between adjacent siblings without affecting the first or last child:

<ul class="space-y-3">
  <li>First item</li>
  <li>Second item</li>  <!-- margin-top: 0.75rem -->
  <li>Third item</li>   <!-- margin-top: 0.75rem -->
</ul>

Building a profile card

A profile card demonstrates the full spacing toolkit: a constrained-width container centred on the page, a card with internal padding, section spacing, and element gaps.

storyBeats.text: Master Ember, the Academy's layout carver, spreads a large sheet of graph paper across a stone table. Each square is exactly four pixels wide.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Ember
storyBeats.text: Every space in the Academy is measured in the same unit: four pixels. You do not guess distances. You choose from the scale — and because every element uses the same scale, the whole page breathes in rhythm.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Ember
storyBeats.text: Two patterns you will use on every page: max-w-7xl mx-auto px-6 — a centred content container with side padding. And gap-4 on a flex or grid parent — gutters between every child, symmetrically, in one place.

Build a profile card layout. The spacing must come entirely from Tailwind utilities — no custom CSS.

  • .container: max-w-lg, mx-auto, px-6, py-8
  • .card: bg-white, rounded-2xl, shadow-lg, p-8
  • .card-header: mb-6
  • .card-name: text-2xl, font-bold, text-gray-900
  • .card-role: text-sm, text-gray-500, mt-1
  • .card-stats: flex, gap-6, mt-4

Rebuild this profile card layout from memory — you know the spacing system, now prove it.

  • The .container should be constrained in width (large, but not full page), centred horizontally, with horizontal and vertical padding.
  • The .card needs generous inner padding, very rounded corners, and a prominent shadow.
  • The .card-header needs a bottom margin to visually separate it from the stats.

Remember: spacing number × 4 = pixels.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain Tailwind's spacing scale to a designer who is used to working with Figma's 8-point grid. How do the Tailwind spacing numbers map to their existing workflow? At what points do they differ, and what is the practical impact?

questions.questionHtml: What pixel value does p-6 represent?
questions.explanationHtml: Tailwind's spacing scale uses a 4px base unit. p-6 = 6 × 4px = 24px (1.5rem). The most important values to memorise are: p-2=8px, p-4=16px, p-6=24px, p-8=32px.

questions.questionHtml: Which class centres a block element horizontally within its parent?
questions.explanationHtml: mx-auto applies margin-left: auto and margin-right: auto, which centres a block element horizontally. It requires the element to have a defined width (such as max-w-*). text-center aligns inline text, not the element itself.

questions.questionHtml: You want a page content column that is at most 1280px wide, centred on the page, with 24px of horizontal padding on each side. Which class combination achieves this?
questions.explanationHtml: max-w-7xl caps the width at 1280px, mx-auto centres it, and px-6 adds 24px of horizontal padding (6 × 4px). This is the most common page-level container pattern in Tailwind projects.

questions.questionHtml: A flex container has three child elements. You want 16px of space between each child. Which approach is preferred in Tailwind?
options: mr-4 on every child except the last
ml-4 on every child except the first
questions.explanationHtml: gap-4 on the flex parent is the correct approach. It is symmetric (applies between all children without affecting outer edges), and changing the gap requires editing only one class in one place. Applying margins to individual children is fragile — removing a child breaks the spacing logic.

questions.questionHtml: What is max-w-prose optimised for, and what is its approximate value?
questions.explanationHtml: max-w-prose sets max-width: 65ch, which is approximately 65 characters per line — the range typographers consider optimal for reading comfort. Use it for article body text, blog posts, and documentation pages. It scales with the font size, which is why it uses ch units rather than pixels.

subChunks.title: Colour and Typography
subChunks.hookHtml: A developer who can reach for the right shade of gray instantly, set a typographic hierarchy in under a minute, and understand why text-blue-600/75 means 75% opacity — that developer ships UI significantly faster than one who guesses hex codes.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The colour palette

Tailwind ships 22 colour families. Every team project customises this, but the defaults are excellent starting points:

slate  gray  zinc  neutral  stone   ← grays
red  orange  amber  yellow          ← warm
lime  green  emerald  teal  cyan    ← cool greens
sky  blue  indigo  violet  purple   ← blues/purples
fuchsia  pink  rose                 ← pinks

Each family has 11 shades: 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, 950.

  • 50 — near white, barely tinted. Good for page backgrounds.
  • 100–200 — light tints. Good for subtle card backgrounds, chips.
  • 400–600 — vivid mid-range. Good for buttons, links, icons.
  • 700–800 — dark shades. Good for text on light backgrounds.
  • 900–950 — near black. Good for headings, dark mode backgrounds.

Using colour utilities

bg-blue-500       /* background-color */
text-blue-700     /* color             */
border-blue-300   /* border-color      */
ring-blue-500     /* outline ring      */

/* Opacity modifier (Tailwind v3+) */
text-blue-600/75  /* color at 75% opacity */
bg-black/50       /* black background at 50% opacity */

Typography: font size

Tailwind's type scale is based on rem units:

text-xs    →  12px  (0.75rem)
text-sm    →  14px  (0.875rem)
text-base  →  16px  (1rem)       ← browser default
text-lg    →  18px  (1.125rem)
text-xl    →  20px  (1.25rem)
text-2xl   →  24px  (1.5rem)
text-3xl   →  30px  (1.875rem)
text-4xl   →  36px  (2.25rem)
text-5xl   →  48px  (3rem)
text-6xl   →  60px  (3.75rem)
text-7xl   →  72px  (4.5rem)
text-8xl   →  96px  (6rem)
text-9xl   →  128px (8rem)

Typography: font weight

font-thin       →  100
font-extralight →  200
font-light      →  300
font-normal     →  400
font-medium     →  500
font-semibold   →  600
font-bold       →  700
font-extrabold  →  800
font-black      →  900

Typography: line-height (leading)

leading-none     →  1       (tight headings)
leading-tight    →  1.25
leading-snug     →  1.375
leading-normal   →  1.5     (body text default)
leading-relaxed  →  1.625   (comfortable reading)
leading-loose    →  2

Typography: letter-spacing (tracking)

tracking-tighter  →  -0.05em
tracking-tight    →  -0.025em
tracking-normal   →  0em
tracking-wide     →  0.025em
tracking-wider    →  0.05em
tracking-widest   →  0.1em   (all-caps labels)

Text alignment

text-left    text-center    text-right    text-justify

A complete typographic hierarchy in React

function BlogPost({ tag, title, author, date, intro }) {
  return (
    <article className="max-w-prose mx-auto py-12 px-6">
      <span className="bg-violet-100 text-violet-700 text-xs font-semibold
                       px-3 py-1 rounded-full tracking-wide uppercase">
        {tag}
      </span>

      <h1 className="text-4xl font-bold leading-tight text-gray-900 mt-4">
        {title}
      </h1>

      <p className="text-sm text-gray-400 mt-2">
        By {author} — {date}
      </p>

      <p className="text-lg leading-relaxed text-gray-700 mt-6">
        {intro}
      </p>
    </article>
  );
}

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: Colour is not decoration. It is information. The shade tells the reader what to feel: 50 whispers. 500 speaks clearly. 900 commands attention. Learn the scale and you will never guess a hex code again.

storyBeats.speaker: The shade scale — 50 is near-white, 950 is near-black
storyBeats.text:

bg-blue-500  ← vivid blue, buttons and links
bg-blue-900  ← deep blue, dark headings

/* Opacity modifier — Tailwind v3+ */

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: Typography follows the same discipline. A heading is not just big — it is text-4xl font-bold leading-tight. Body text is not just normal — it is text-base leading-relaxed text-gray-700. Every decision is explicit and shared.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: You are building a design system for a SaaS product. Explain how you would use Tailwind's colour palette to create a consistent, accessible colour system — covering primary actions, semantic states (success, warning, error), and neutral text hierarchy. Which shade numbers would you reach for and why?

questions.questionHtml: In Tailwind's colour scale, what kind of colour is shade 50?
options: A very light, near-white tint of the colour
The most vivid, saturated version of the colour
A near-black dark shade of the colour
The neutral gray version of the colour
questions.correctAnswer: A very light, near-white tint of the colour
questions.explanationHtml: The shade scale runs from 50 (near-white, barely tinted) up to 950 (near-black). Shade 50 is almost always a page or card background tone. Shades 400–600 are the vivid mid-range used for buttons and interactive elements. Shades 700–900 are used for text on light backgrounds.

questions.questionHtml: What does leading-relaxed control in Tailwind?
options: Line-height (the vertical spacing between lines of text)
questions.correctAnswer: Line-height (the vertical spacing between lines of text)
questions.explanationHtml: The leading-* utilities control line-height. leading-relaxed sets line-height: 1.625, which gives body text comfortable breathing room. For comparison: leading-tight (1.25) is used for headings; leading-normal (1.5) is the default.

questions.questionHtml: You want an article heading that is 36px, black (#111), bold, with tight line spacing. Which class combination is correct?
questions.explanationHtml: text-4xl (36px), font-bold (700 weight), leading-tight (1.25 line-height), text-gray-900 (very dark gray — more refined than pure black for headings). This is a real typographic pattern you will use repeatedly in production work.

questions.questionHtml: What does text-emerald-600/50 do?
options: Sets the text colour to emerald-600 at 50% opacity
Sets both the text colour (emerald-600) and background opacity (50%)
Sets the text colour to a 50/50 mix of emerald-600 and white
Applies emerald-600 to every other character
questions.correctAnswer: Sets the text colour to emerald-600 at 50% opacity
questions.explanationHtml: The slash modifier (/N) appended to any colour utility sets the opacity of that specific property. text-emerald-600/50 is equivalent to setting color: rgb(5 150 105 / 0.5). This works with bg-*, border-*, and ring-* utilities too. It replaces the older text-opacity-* approach from Tailwind v2 and is the standard way to apply opacity to any colour utility.

questions.questionHtml: A designer hands you a Figma spec with five text colours: #111827 (headings), #374151 (body), #6B7280 (captions), #9CA3AF (placeholders), and #D1D5DB (disabled). Without checking the Tailwind source, which palette family and which shade numbers best match this spec?
options: gray-900, gray-700, gray-500, gray-400, gray-300 — these are the Tailwind gray scale values
slate-900, slate-700, slate-500, slate-400, slate-300 — slate is always darker than gray
zinc-950, zinc-800, zinc-600, zinc-400, zinc-200 — zinc skews cooler
questions.correctAnswer: gray-900, gray-700, gray-500, gray-400, gray-300 — these are the Tailwind gray scale values
questions.explanationHtml: Those hex values are the exact default Tailwind gray palette: gray-900=#111827, gray-700=#374151, gray-500=#6B7280, gray-400=#9CA3AF, gray-300=#D1D5DB. This is not coincidence — Tailwind's designers tuned the gray scale for exactly this kind of multi-level text hierarchy. Recognising this mapping is a real productivity skill: when a designer gives you grays from a Figma file using Tailwind's defaults, you can translate directly to class names without colour picking.

subChunks.title: Flexbox Layout
subChunks.hookHtml: Flexbox is one of the two layout primitives that power nearly every UI on the web (the other is Grid, which comes in B-tier). If you can build a nav bar, a card with side-by-side content, and a centered hero — you can build most of what a junior front-end role demands.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Activating flex

flex         /* display: flex         */
inline-flex  /* display: inline-flex  */

Flex direction

flex-row          /* default — children go left to right */
flex-col          /* children stack top to bottom        */
flex-row-reverse  /* right to left                       */
flex-col-reverse  /* bottom to top                       */

Align items (cross axis)

items-start     /* align-items: flex-start  */
items-center    /* align-items: center      */
items-end       /* align-items: flex-end    */
items-stretch   /* align-items: stretch (default) */
items-baseline  /* align-items: baseline    */

Justify content (main axis)

justify-start    /* flex-start  */
justify-center   /* center      */
justify-end      /* flex-end    */
justify-between  /* space-between — first item left, last right, equal gaps between */
justify-around   /* space-around  */
justify-evenly   /* space-evenly  */

Flex wrap

flex-wrap         /* children wrap to next line when needed */
flex-nowrap       /* children never wrap (default)          */
flex-wrap-reverse /* wrap, but new lines appear above        */

Flex children: how they grow and shrink

flex-1     /* flex: 1 1 0   — grows AND shrinks to fill available space */
flex-auto  /* flex: 1 1 auto — grows and shrinks based on content size  */
flex-none  /* flex: none    — fixed size, never grows or shrinks        */
grow       /* flex-grow: 1  — grows but does not change shrink          */
shrink-0   /* flex-shrink: 0 — prevents shrinking                      */

Individual alignment override

self-auto    self-start    self-center    self-end    self-stretch

Order

order-first  order-last  order-none  order-1  order-2  /* ...up to order-12 */

Pattern 1: Navigation bar

The classic nav bar uses justify-between to push the logo left and the CTA right, with items-center for vertical alignment:

<nav className="flex justify-between items-center px-6 py-4 bg-white border-b border-gray-100">
  <a className="font-bold text-xl text-gray-900">Arcane Academy</a>

  <div className="flex gap-6">
    <a className="text-sm text-gray-600 hover:text-gray-900">Topics</a>
    <a className="text-sm text-gray-600 hover:text-gray-900">Reviews</a>
    <a className="text-sm text-gray-600 hover:text-gray-900">Profile</a>
  </div>

  <button className="bg-blue-600 text-white text-sm font-medium px-4 py-2 rounded-md">
    Start Learning
  </button>
</nav>

Pattern 2: Horizontal card (image + content)

<div className="flex gap-4 items-start bg-white rounded-xl p-6 shadow-sm">
  <img
    src="/avatar.jpg"
    className="w-16 h-16 rounded-full flex-none object-cover"
  />
  <div className="flex-1 min-w-0">
    <h3 className="font-semibold text-gray-900 truncate">Aria Sunforge</h3>
    <p className="text-sm text-gray-500 mt-1 leading-relaxed">
      Senior Enchanter — 142 quests completed
    </p>
  </div>
</div>

Key insight: flex-none on the image prevents it from shrinking; flex-1 min-w-0 on the content makes it fill the remaining space while allowing text truncation to work correctly.

Gap vs margins on children

Always prefer gap-* on the flex parent over margins on individual children. Gaps are symmetric (no excess margin after the last item), and changing the spacing requires editing one class in one place.

storyBeats.text: Master Ember leads you to a workshop table covered in wooden blocks of different sizes. He begins arranging them in a row.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Ember
storyBeats.text: Every layout is a conversation between a container and its children. The container decides the direction, the alignment, and the distribution. The children decide whether they grow, shrink, or hold firm.

storyBeats.speaker: The three flex decisions you make on every container
storyBeats.text:
flex              /* activate flex */
flex-row          /* direction: horizontal (default) */
items-center      /* cross-axis: vertically centred */
justify-between   /* main-axis: push to edges */

storyBeats.speaker: Master Ember
storyBeats.text: The nav bar is the most-built component in all of front-end work. Logo on the left. Links in the middle. Button on the right. That is justify-between on the container plus a flex gap-6 group for the links. You will build this a hundred times in your career — learn it cold.

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: One more thing: when a child should fill all available space, give it flex-1. When it must stay its natural size no matter what — an avatar, an icon, a logo — give it flex-none. These two classes resolve most flex sizing confusions.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Describe a scenario where you would give a flex child flex-1 versus flex-none. Then explain what happens visually if you use flex-1 on an image that should stay its natural size — and how you would debug it.

questions.questionHtml: Which class distributes flex children so the first is left-aligned, the last is right-aligned, and remaining children are equally spaced in between?
questions.explanationHtml: justify-between applies justify-content: space-between — the first child is flush left, the last is flush right, and the space is divided equally between children. This is the correct class for nav bars, toolbars, and any layout where you want to "push items to the edges."

questions.questionHtml: What does flex-col do?
options: Sets flex-direction to column, so children stack vertically
Collapses the flex container to a single column on mobile
Limits the container to one child per row
questions.correctAnswer: Sets flex-direction to column, so children stack vertically
questions.explanationHtml: flex-col applies flex-direction: column. Combined with flex, children stack from top to bottom. The cross axis becomes horizontal, so items-center centres children horizontally and justify-center centres them vertically.

questions.questionHtml: You have a horizontal card: an avatar image (fixed 64px square) on the left, and a text block on the right that should fill the remaining space. Which utility combination on the two children achieves this?
options: flex-none on the image, flex-1 on the text block
w-16 on the image, w-full on the text block
flex-shrink on the image, flex-grow on the text block
fixed on the image, grow on the text block
questions.correctAnswer: flex-none on the image, flex-1 on the text block
questions.explanationHtml: flex-none (flex: none) prevents the image from growing or shrinking — it stays exactly its natural or specified size. flex-1 (flex: 1 1 0) makes the text block grow to fill all available space. This is the standard pattern for media-object layouts (icon/avatar + content).

questions.questionHtml: Which is the preferred way to add 16px of space between each item in a flex row?
options: mr-4 on every child except the last using :not(:last-child)
ml-4 on every child except the first
space-x-4 applied to each flex child individually
questions.explanationHtml: gap-4 on the container is idiomatic Tailwind. It is: (1) symmetric — no excess space after the last item, (2) easy to change — one value in one place, and (3) works correctly when items wrap. Applying margins to individual children is fragile: adding or removing a child can break the spacing, and the first/last exceptions add complexity.

questions.questionHtml:
A developer is building a card list. Each card has a title, a description, and a "View Details" button. They want the button to always appear at the bottom of the card regardless of how long the title or description is. All cards have equal height in a grid row.

Which flex approach achieves this?
options: Make each card flex-col, then add mt-auto to the button — mt-auto in a flex column pushes the button to the bottom
Make each card position-relative and the button position-absolute bottom-0
Add min-h-full to the button so it stretches to the card's height
Add justify-end to the card and place the button last in the DOM
questions.correctAnswer: Make each card flex-col, then add mt-auto to the button — mt-auto in a flex column pushes the button to the bottom
questions.explanationHtml: This is one of the most useful flex tricks in practice. A flex column with flex-col on the card, combined with mt-auto on the button, consumes all available space above the button with an automatic top margin. The title and description stack normally at the top; the button is always at the bottom. This works correctly regardless of content length and does not require absolute positioning, which would break the normal document flow.
